- Key AI risks: accuracy, bias, privacy, security, misuse, and over-reliance.
- Scale verification to the stakes of the decision.
- Accountability always rests with people.

title: AI & Agent Foundations certification prep course
section: Hallucination, risk, and responsible use › Common pitfalls
text:
Common pitfalls:
- Taking a confident tone or a neat citation as proof of accuracy.
- Asking the same model to verify its own answer.
- Pasting personal or confidential information into unapproved public AI tools.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
text:
Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
A practitioner course on designing, building, evaluating, and operating LLM-based agents. It covers agent architectures and design patterns, tool calling and structured output, planning and memory, production-grade RAG, multi-agent orchestration, evaluation, deployment and scaling, and running agents safely with human oversight.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Agent architecture and design patterns
text:
Module: Agent architecture and design patterns (40 min). Domain: Agent architecture and design.
Objectives:
- Choose between a fixed workflow, a single agent, and a multi-agent system for a given problem
- Apply the common agentic patterns: prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, ReAct, plan-and-execute, reflection, and orchestrator-workers
- Design the agent's control loop, including stop conditions and budgets
- Document an agent design so it can be reviewed

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Agent architecture and design patterns › Start with the simplest thing that works
text:
Start with the simplest thing that works
The most common architecture mistake is building an autonomous agent for a problem a fixed pipeline could solve. Use this ladder and stop at the first rung that meets the requirement:
Single LLM call with a good prompt (and maybe retrieval).
Workflow: several LLM calls and tools connected by code in a fixed or branching order.
Single agent: one model in a loop, choosing tools dynamically.
Multi-agent system: several specialized agents coordinated by an orchestrator.
Each rung adds flexibility and also adds cost, latency, unpredictability, and evaluation difficulty. Move up only when the task genuinely needs run-time decisions that can't be enumerated in advance.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Agent architecture and design patterns › Workflow patterns
text:
Workflow patterns
Pattern
How it works
Use when
Prompt chaining
Output of step 1 feeds step 2, with optional checks ("gates") between steps.
The task decomposes cleanly into fixed stages (outline → draft → edit).
Routing
A classifier (LLM or traditional) sends each input to a specialized prompt, model, or tool.
Inputs fall into distinct categories that need different handling (billing vs. technical support).
Parallelization
Independent subtasks run simultaneously (sectioning), or the same task runs several times and results are combined (voting).
Speed matters, or you want multiple perspectives or a majority vote.
Evaluator–optimizer
One call generates, another critiques against criteria, and the loop repeats until criteria are met.
Clear quality criteria exist and iteration measurably helps (translation, code that must pass tests).

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Agent architecture and design patterns › Agent patterns
text:
Agent patterns
ReAct interleaves a reasoning step with each tool call (Thought → Action → Observation). It is flexible and transparent, but it decides one step at a time and can wander on long tasks.
Plan-and-execute first produces an explicit multi-step plan, then executes steps (possibly with a cheaper model), and re-plans if a step fails or new information arrives. It is better for long tasks, and the plan itself can be reviewed by a human before anything runs.
Reflection (self-critique) has the agent review its own output or trajectory against criteria and revise. It catches many mistakes but cannot catch errors the model is systematically blind to; external checks (tests, validators, retrieval) are stronger.
Orchestrator–workers uses a central agent that breaks a goal into subtasks at run time and delegates them to worker agents or tools, then synthesizes results. Covered in depth in Module 5.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Agent architecture and design patterns › Designing the control loop
text:
Designing the control loop
Every agent loop needs explicit answers to these questions before it ships:
Stop conditions: what counts as done? The model declaring a final answer, a validator passing, or a human approving.
Budgets: maximum iterations, tokens, wall-clock time, and spend per task. Hitting a budget should end the run gracefully with a partial result and a clear status, not crash.
Error handling: what happens when a tool times out, returns an error, or returns nonsense? Retry with backoff, try an alternative, or escalate.
Escalation: when does the agent hand off to a human?
State: what is kept between steps, and where (in context, in a state object, in external storage)?
# Illustrative agent loop with budgets and stop conditions
def run_agent(goal, tools, max_steps=8, max_cost_usd=0.50):
state = {"goal": goal, "history": [], "cost": 0.0}
for step in range(max_steps):
decision = llm_decide(state, tools) # thought + chosen action
state["cost"] += decision.cost

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Agent architecture and design patterns › Designing the control loop

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Agent architecture and design patterns › Choosing models for each role
text:
Choosing models for each role
Not every step needs the most capable model. A common design uses a strong reasoning model for planning and difficult judgment, and smaller, faster models for routing, extraction, and summarization. This can cut cost and latency dramatically. Make the model a configurable parameter of each step so you can swap models after evaluation (Module 6).

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Agent architecture and design patterns › Write it down: the agent design document
text:
Write it down: the agent design document
Before building, capture a one- or two-page design: the goal and success criteria; users; the chosen pattern and why simpler options were rejected; tools and their permission levels; data sources; memory strategy; budgets and stop conditions; human checkpoints; known risks and mitigations; and how it will be evaluated and monitored. This document becomes the basis for review, testing, and the governance record in Module 8.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Agent architecture and design patterns › Key takeaways
text:
Key takeaways:
- Climb the complexity ladder only as far as the task requires: call → workflow → agent → multi-agent.
- Workflow patterns: chaining, routing, parallelization, evaluator–optimizer.
- Agent patterns: ReAct, plan-and-execute, reflection, orchestrator–workers.
- Every loop needs stop conditions, budgets, error handling, and escalation paths.
- Assign models per step based on difficulty, cost, and latency.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Agent architecture and design patterns › Common pitfalls
text:
Common pitfalls:
- Jumping to multi-agent designs because they sound advanced, not because the task needs them.
- Loops with no iteration, cost, or time budget.
- Relying on self-reflection alone when an external validator (tests, schema checks, retrieval) is available.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Agent development: tools, function calling, and structured output
text:
Module: Agent development: tools, function calling, and structured output (45 min). Domain: Agent development.
Objectives:
- Define tools with clear names, descriptions, and JSON-schema parameters
- Implement the tool-calling loop, including parallel calls and error results
- Enforce and validate structured output
- Apply production practices: timeouts, retries, idempotency, and sandboxing

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Agent development: tools, function calling, and structured output › Defining a tool

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Agent development: tools, function calling, and structured output › Defining a tool
text: Good tool design: one clear purpose per tool; names that read like verbs; enums instead of free text where possible; descriptions that say when not to use the tool; and outputs that are concise and relevant (huge tool outputs waste context and distract the model).

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Agent development: tools, function calling, and structured output › The tool-calling loop
text:
The tool-calling loop
Most model APIs, including the widely used OpenAI-compatible format, follow the same flow:
Send the conversation plus the list of tool definitions.
The model replies with either a final message or one or more tool calls (name + JSON arguments + an ID).
Your code validates the arguments, executes each call, and appends a tool result message referencing the call ID.
Send the updated conversation back. Repeat until the model returns a final message.
# Illustrative; exact field names vary by SDK
messages = [system_msg, user_msg]
while True:
resp = client.chat(model=MODEL, messages=messages, tools=TOOLS)
msg = resp.message
messages.append(msg)
if not msg.tool_calls:
break # final answer
for call in msg.tool_calls: # may be several in parallel
try:
args = validate(call.name, json.loads(call.arguments))
result = REGISTRY[call.name](**args)
content = json.dumps(result)[:4000] # keep results compact
except Exception as e:

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Agent development: tools, function calling, and structured output › The tool-calling loop
text:
content = json.dumps({"error": str(e)}) # let the model recover
messages.append({"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": call.id,
"content": content})
Return errors to the model as tool results rather than crashing: models are often good at correcting a malformed argument or choosing a different approach once they see the error.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Agent development: tools, function calling, and structured output › Structured output
text:
Structured output
When an agent's output is consumed by code, free text is fragile. Use the strongest mechanism available:
Schema-constrained decoding (often called structured outputs or guided decoding): the inference engine only allows tokens that keep the output valid against your JSON Schema. Most reliable.
JSON mode: guarantees valid JSON, but not your specific schema.
Prompt instructions plus examples: weakest; works most of the time.
Whatever the mechanism, validate the result in code (for example with Pydantic or a JSON Schema validator). On failure, retry once with the validation error included in the prompt, then fail clearly.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Agent development: tools, function calling, and structured output › Production practices for tools
text:
Production practices for tools
Timeouts on every external call; agents stall silently without them.
Retries with exponential backoff for transient errors (rate limits, network blips) — but only for safe operations.
Idempotency: design write operations so repeating them doesn't duplicate effects (e.g., an idempotency key on "create payment"). Agents and retry logic will repeat calls.
Least privilege: each tool gets only the permissions it needs — a read-only database user for a lookup tool.
Sandboxing: run model-generated code in an isolated environment with no network or file access beyond what is needed, and with CPU/memory/time limits.
Input validation: never pass model-generated arguments directly into SQL, shell commands, or file paths. Treat them as untrusted user input.
Logging: record every call, its arguments, result summary, latency, and cost.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Agent development: tools, function calling, and structured output › Frameworks and standards
text:
Frameworks and standards
You can build agents with plain API calls, which keeps everything visible. Frameworks add structure: LangGraph models agents as state graphs with explicit nodes and edges; CrewAI organizes role-based agent teams; AutoGen focuses on conversational multi-agent setups; and LlamaIndex is strong on data and retrieval. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes how tools and data sources are exposed to agents, so a tool server written once can be used by many clients.
Choose a framework for what it makes easier (state management, persistence, human-in-the-loop interrupts, tracing), and make sure you can still see the exact prompts and tool calls it sends.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Agent development: tools, function calling, and structured output › Key takeaways
text:
Key takeaways:
- Tool descriptions are prompts: say what the tool does, when to use it, and when not to.
- The model proposes tool calls; your code validates, executes, and returns results with matching IDs.
- Return tool errors to the model so it can recover.
- Prefer schema-constrained structured output, and always validate in code.
- Timeouts, backoff, idempotency, least privilege, sandboxing, and logging are mandatory in production.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Agent development: tools, function calling, and structured output › Common pitfalls
text:
Common pitfalls:
- Vague tool descriptions, so the model calls the wrong tool or none at all.
- Passing model-generated arguments directly into SQL or shell commands.
- Retrying non-idempotent write operations and causing duplicate actions.
- Dumping enormous tool outputs into context.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Cognition, planning, and memory
text:
Module: Cognition, planning, and memory (40 min). Domain: Cognition, planning, and memory.
Objectives:
- Apply task decomposition and planning strategies, including re-planning
- Use reasoning techniques: chain-of-thought, self-consistency, and reasoning models
- Design short-term and long-term memory: buffers, summaries, episodic, semantic, and procedural memory
- Manage the context window deliberately (context engineering)

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Cognition, planning, and memory › Planning and decomposition
text:
Planning and decomposition
Agents succeed on complex goals by breaking them down. Common strategies:
Upfront decomposition: generate a list of subtasks with dependencies before acting (plan-and-execute).
Hierarchical planning: high-level steps first, each expanded into detailed steps only when reached.
Interleaved planning: decide one step at a time based on the latest observation (ReAct).
Re-planning: when a step fails or results contradict assumptions, revise the remaining plan rather than pushing on.
Represent plans as structured data (a list of steps with status, inputs, and outputs) rather than prose. Structured plans can be displayed to users, checkpointed, resumed after a crash, and audited.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Cognition, planning, and memory › Reasoning techniques
text:
Reasoning techniques
Chain-of-thought prompting asks for intermediate reasoning and improves multi-step accuracy. Self-consistency samples several independent reasoning paths and takes the majority answer, trading cost for reliability. Tree-of-thought-style search explores and scores multiple partial solutions. Many current models are reasoning models that perform extended internal reasoning before answering; for these, give clear goals and constraints rather than step-by-step instructions, and budget for the extra latency and tokens.
Design choice: reserve expensive reasoning for decisions that need it — planning, ambiguous judgment, debugging — and use fast models for routine steps.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Cognition, planning, and memory › Types of memory
text:
Types of memory
Memory type
Holds
Typical implementation
Working (short-term)
The current task: recent messages, tool results, the plan
The context window
Episodic
What happened in past sessions — "last week the user asked for a shorter report"
Stored conversation summaries or event logs, retrieved by relevance or recency
Semantic
Facts and knowledge: user preferences, domain facts, entity details
Key-value stores, databases, vector indexes, knowledge graphs
Procedural
How to do things: instructions, learned routines, reusable skills
The system prompt, stored prompt templates or skill files, tool definitions

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Cognition, planning, and memory › Managing the context window
text:
Managing the context window
Context engineering means deciding what goes into the limited context window at each step. Useful techniques:
Sliding window: keep only the last N turns.
Summarization: compress older turns into a running summary; keep recent turns verbatim.
Retrieval: store everything externally and pull in only what's relevant to the current step.
Scratchpads and notes: let the agent write key findings to an external file or state object, then reload just those notes.
Tool-output trimming: return summaries or the relevant fields instead of entire documents.
Sub-agents: give a sub-task its own fresh context and return only a condensed result to the parent.
Long contexts are not free: they raise cost and latency, and models can attend less reliably to details buried in the middle. More context is not always better context.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Cognition, planning, and memory › Writing to long-term memory safely
text:
Writing to long-term memory safely
Memory that persists across sessions needs rules: what is worth storing (stable preferences and facts, not every message), who can read it (per-user isolation), how long it is kept (retention limits), and how a user can view and delete it. Memory is also an attack surface: if an agent stores content from an untrusted web page as a "fact", that poisoned memory can influence every future session. Validate before storing, and record the source of each memory.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Cognition, planning, and memory › Key takeaways
text:
Key takeaways:
- Decompose goals into structured plans and re-plan when reality diverges.
- Chain-of-thought, self-consistency, and reasoning models trade cost for accuracy — use them where it matters.
- Memory types: working, episodic, semantic, procedural.
- Context engineering: summarize, retrieve, trim, and isolate rather than accumulate.
- Long-term memory needs scope, retention, user control, and protection against poisoning.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Cognition, planning, and memory › Common pitfalls
text:
Common pitfalls:
- Pushing on with a plan after a step has clearly failed instead of re-planning.
- Stuffing the entire history into context until it overflows or becomes costly and confused.
- Storing unverified external content as long-term memory.
- Mixing different users' memories in a shared store without isolation.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Knowledge integration: production RAG and data handling
text:
Module: Knowledge integration: production RAG and data handling (45 min). Domain: Knowledge integration and data handling.
Objectives:
- Build an ingestion pipeline: parsing, cleaning, chunking, metadata, and embedding
- Improve retrieval with hybrid search, reranking, query rewriting, and metadata filtering
- Explain agentic RAG and when to use knowledge graphs or SQL instead of vectors
- Handle data responsibly: access control, PII, freshness, and provenance

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Knowledge integration: production RAG and data handling › The RAG pipeline end to end
text:
The RAG pipeline end to end
Production RAG has two pipelines. Ingestion (offline): load documents → parse (PDF, HTML, tables, scans via OCR) → clean → chunk → attach metadata → embed → store in a vector index. Query (online): receive question → optionally rewrite it → retrieve candidates → rerank → assemble context → generate with citations → validate.
Most RAG quality problems are retrieval problems: if the right passage never reaches the model, no prompt can fix the answer. Evaluate retrieval separately from generation (Module 6).

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Knowledge integration: production RAG and data handling › Chunking strategies
text:
Chunking strategies
Strategy
Description
Trade-off
Fixed-size
Split every N tokens with some overlap (e.g., 500 tokens, 50 overlap)
Simple, but can cut ideas in half
Structure-aware
Split on headings, sections, paragraphs, or table boundaries
Keeps meaning together; needs good parsing
Semantic
Split where the topic shifts, based on embedding similarity
Coherent chunks; more compute
Parent–child
Retrieve small chunks for precision, then pass their larger parent section for context
Precise and complete; more complex
Attach metadata to each chunk: source, title, section, date, author, access level. Metadata enables filtering ("only 2025 policies"), citations, and permission checks.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Knowledge integration: production RAG and data handling › Better retrieval
text:
Better retrieval
Hybrid search: combine dense vector search (meaning) with sparse keyword search such as BM25 (exact terms like product codes, names, error IDs), then fuse the rankings.
Reranking: retrieve a broad set (e.g., top 50) cheaply, then use a cross-encoder reranker model to score each candidate against the query and keep the best 5–10. This is often the single biggest quality gain.
Query rewriting: turn conversational follow-ups ("what about for contractors?") into standalone queries; expand acronyms; generate several query variants.
Metadata filtering: restrict search by date, department, product, or the user's permissions before ranking.
Embedding model choice: domain and language matter; evaluate candidate embedding and reranking models on your own queries rather than relying on public leaderboards.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Knowledge integration: production RAG and data handling › Agentic RAG and other knowledge sources
text:
Agentic RAG and other knowledge sources
In basic RAG, retrieval happens once. In agentic RAG, retrieval is a tool the agent chooses to call — possibly several times, with refined queries, across several sources — and it judges whether results are sufficient before answering. This handles multi-hop questions ("Which of our suppliers in Germany had late deliveries last quarter?") far better.
Vectors aren't always the right store. Use SQL or APIs for structured, exact data (counts, totals, filters) — let the agent generate a query against a read-only, permission-scoped connection. Use a knowledge graph when relationships between entities matter (GraphRAG). Many systems combine all three.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Knowledge integration: production RAG and data handling › Grounded generation and citations
text:
Grounded generation and citations
Instruct the model to answer only from the provided context, cite the chunk ID for each claim, and say when the context is insufficient. Then check: verify cited IDs exist in the retrieved set, and for high-stakes uses run a groundedness check that each claim is supported by its citation.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Knowledge integration: production RAG and data handling › Responsible data handling
text:
Responsible data handling
Access control at retrieval time: a user must only retrieve chunks they are permitted to see. Enforce this in the retrieval query, never by asking the model to withhold information.
PII: detect and redact or exclude personal data during ingestion where it isn't needed.
Freshness: re-ingest changed documents, delete removed ones, and store dates so stale content can be filtered or flagged.
Provenance: know where every chunk came from and when; this underpins citations, audits, and deletion requests.
Untrusted content: documents can contain hidden instructions (indirect prompt injection). Treat retrieved text as data, not commands.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Knowledge integration: production RAG and data handling › Key takeaways
text:
Key takeaways:
- RAG = ingestion (parse, chunk, embed, store) + query (rewrite, retrieve, rerank, generate, validate).
- Chunk along document structure and attach rich metadata.
- Hybrid search plus reranking is the standard recipe for strong retrieval.
- Agentic RAG lets the agent search iteratively across sources; use SQL and graphs where they fit.
- Enforce permissions, PII handling, freshness, and provenance in the data layer.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Knowledge integration: production RAG and data handling › Common pitfalls
text:
Common pitfalls:
- Tuning the generation prompt when the real problem is that retrieval never finds the right chunk.
- Relying on the model to hide documents a user isn't allowed to see.
- Vector search for questions that need exact aggregation — use SQL.
- Never re-indexing, so answers cite outdated policies.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Multi-agent systems and orchestration
text:
Module: Multi-agent systems and orchestration (35 min). Domain: Agent architecture and design.
Objectives:
- Compare multi-agent topologies: orchestrator–worker, hierarchical, sequential, and peer collaboration
- Design reliable handoffs with structured contracts and verification
- Recognize multi-agent failure modes such as error compounding, loops, and context loss
- Decide when multiple agents are worth their extra cost

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Multi-agent systems and orchestration › Why multiple agents?
text:
Why multiple agents?
Splitting work across agents helps when subtasks need different tools, instructions, or models; when they can run in parallel; or when one agent's context would overflow. Each agent gets a focused role, a smaller toolset, and a clean context, which often improves reliability. The price is more LLM calls, more latency, and more places for things to go wrong.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Multi-agent systems and orchestration › Topologies
text:
Topologies
Topology
Shape
Good for
Orchestrator–worker
A lead agent decomposes the goal, delegates to workers, and synthesizes results
Research, analysis, tasks whose subtasks aren't known in advance
Sequential pipeline
Agent A → Agent B → Agent C
Content workflows: research → draft → fact-check → publish
Hierarchical
Managers supervising teams of workers, several levels deep
Very large tasks; rarely needed
Peer / debate
Agents critique or negotiate with each other
Surfacing disagreement, red-teaming, decision review

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Multi-agent systems and orchestration › Handoffs are contracts
text:
Handoffs are contracts
A handoff is where one agent's output becomes another's input. Treat it as an API contract:
Define a schema for what passes between agents (fields, types, required evidence such as source URLs).
Validate at each boundary; reject or return malformed output.
Pass the task, not the whole history: give workers a clear brief (objective, constraints, expected output format, budget) so they don't inherit irrelevant context.
Include provenance: which agent produced what, from which sources.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Multi-agent systems and orchestration › Failure modes
text:
Failure modes
Error compounding: a wrong fact from the researcher becomes a polished paragraph and then a published claim. Each stage makes the error look more credible. Mitigation: verification agents or validators between stages, and evidence requirements.
Infinite delegation or ping-pong: agents keep handing work back and forth. Mitigation: global step and cost budgets, and a single owner for termination.
Duplicated or conflicting work: two workers do the same task or contradict each other. Mitigation: clear task boundaries in the orchestrator's briefs.
Lost context: a worker lacks information the orchestrator assumed it had. Mitigation: explicit briefs.
Responsibility diffusion: no single component owns the final answer. Mitigation: the orchestrator (and ultimately a human owner) is accountable for the synthesized result.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Multi-agent systems and orchestration › Observability across agents
text:
Observability across agents
Debugging a multi-agent run without tracing is nearly impossible. Use distributed tracing: one trace per user request, with spans for each agent, LLM call, and tool call, including inputs, outputs, tokens, latency, and cost. Tools such as LangSmith, Langfuse, Arize Phoenix, and OpenTelemetry-based tracing provide this view (Module 8).

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Multi-agent systems and orchestration › Key takeaways
text:
Key takeaways:
- Use multiple agents for specialization, parallelism, or context isolation — not by default.
- Orchestrator–worker and sequential pipelines are the most common topologies.
- Handoffs need schemas, validation, focused briefs, and provenance.
- Error compounding is the defining multi-agent risk; verify between stages.
- Trace every agent, LLM call, and tool call under one request ID.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Multi-agent systems and orchestration › Common pitfalls
text:
Common pitfalls:
- Adding agents to look sophisticated when a single agent with good tools would do.
- Passing unvalidated free text between agents.
- No global budget across the whole multi-agent run.
- No verification step between generating content and publishing it.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Evaluation and tuning
text:
Module: Evaluation and tuning (45 min). Domain: Evaluation and tuning.
Objectives:
- Build an evaluation dataset and define task-specific success metrics
- Evaluate final outputs, retrieval quality, and agent trajectories
- Use LLM-as-a-judge responsibly alongside human review
- Tune agents through prompts, tools, retrieval, model choice, and fine-tuning

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Evaluation and tuning › Evaluation is the core engineering discipline
text:
Evaluation is the core engineering discipline
Agents are non-deterministic and fail in subtle ways, so "it worked when I tried it" is meaningless. Every change to a prompt, model, tool, or retrieval setting should be measured against a fixed evaluation set before release. This is often called eval-driven development.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Evaluation and tuning › Building an evaluation set
text:
Building an evaluation set
Start with 30–100 realistic tasks; grow it over time.
Include the common cases, the edge cases, adversarial inputs, and questions the agent should refuse or say it can't answer.
Add every real production failure as a new test case (regression tests).
For each case, record the expected outcome: a reference answer, required facts, required tool calls, or a rubric.
Keep a held-out portion you don't tune against, to avoid overfitting your prompts to the test set.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Evaluation and tuning › What to measure
text:
What to measure
Level
Example metrics
Final output
Task success rate; correctness vs. reference; rubric scores for helpfulness, tone, completeness; format validity
Retrieval (RAG)
Recall@k (was the right chunk retrieved?); precision; MRR / nDCG (was it ranked high?)
Generation (RAG)
Faithfulness / groundedness (claims supported by context); answer relevance; citation accuracy
Trajectory
Correct tools chosen; correct arguments; unnecessary steps; loops; policy violations along the way
Operational
Latency (time to first token, total), tokens and cost per task, error and timeout rate
Safety
Refusal correctness, prompt-injection resistance, PII leakage, harmful content rate
Because outputs vary, run each case several times and report rates (e.g., "succeeds 9 of 10 runs"), not single results.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Evaluation and tuning › LLM-as-a-judge
text:
LLM-as-a-judge
Grading open-ended output by hand doesn't scale, so a strong model is often used as a judge with a rubric. Make judges trustworthy:
Give a specific rubric with defined score levels, and ask for reasoning before the score.
Prefer pairwise comparison (A vs. B) or binary checks ("Is every claim supported by the context? yes/no") over vague 1–10 scales.
Watch for known biases: preference for longer answers, for the first option shown, and for outputs from the same model family.
Calibrate against human labels on a sample and measure agreement before trusting the judge.
Use deterministic checks (exact match, schema validation, unit tests, regex) wherever possible; they are cheaper and more reliable than any judge.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Evaluation and tuning › Tuning levers, in order
text:
Tuning levers, in order
Prompts and tool descriptions — cheapest and fastest.
Retrieval — chunking, hybrid search, reranking, metadata filters.
Architecture — add a validation step, split a step, change the pattern.
Model choice and inference settings — larger or reasoning model for hard steps; smaller model where quality holds.
Fine-tuning — supervised fine-tuning or parameter-efficient methods (LoRA) on high-quality examples, or preference tuning; useful for consistent format, style, domain language, or tool-use reliability on a smaller model. Fine-tuning is the most expensive lever and requires re-evaluation.
Change one thing at a time and compare against the baseline on the full eval set. Watch for regressions in other categories, not just improvement in the one you targeted.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Evaluation and tuning › Key takeaways
text:
Key takeaways:
- Measure every change against a fixed, growing evaluation set.
- Evaluate outputs, retrieval, trajectories, operations, and safety.
- Report success rates over multiple runs, not single samples.
- LLM judges need rubrics, bias awareness, and calibration against humans.
- Tune in order: prompts → retrieval → architecture → model → fine-tuning.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Evaluation and tuning › Common pitfalls
text:
Common pitfalls:
- Testing on a handful of hand-picked examples.
- Trusting an uncalibrated LLM judge.
- Measuring only the final answer and missing unsafe or wasteful trajectories.
- Fine-tuning before exhausting prompt, retrieval, and architecture changes.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Deployment and scaling
text:
Module: Deployment and scaling (40 min). Domain: Deployment and scaling.
Objectives:
- Explain the latency, throughput, and cost characteristics of LLM inference
- Apply optimization techniques: batching, KV caching, quantization, prompt caching, and model routing
- Describe the layers of a production agent stack: inference serving, model gateway, retrieval services, guardrails, and observability
- Plan a production deployment with scaling, reliability, and cost controls

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Deployment and scaling › How inference performance is measured
text:
How inference performance is measured
Metric
Meaning
Why it matters
Time to first token (TTFT)
Delay before output starts streaming
Perceived responsiveness; driven by input length and queueing
Inter-token latency / tokens per second
Generation speed per request
How fast long answers complete
Throughput
Total tokens or requests per second across all users
How many users a deployment supports; cost per token
End-to-end task latency
Total time for an agent to finish, across all LLM and tool calls
Agents multiply latency: 8 sequential calls at 2 s each is 16 s
For agents, the number of sequential steps usually dominates latency. Reducing steps (better tools, parallel calls, smaller models for simple steps) often matters more than raw model speed.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Deployment and scaling › Optimization techniques
text:
Optimization techniques
Continuous (in-flight) batching: the server interleaves many requests on the GPU, raising throughput substantially.
KV caching: stores attention computations for tokens already processed so each new token doesn't recompute the whole sequence.
Prompt / prefix caching: reuses computation for a shared prefix (like a long system prompt or tool list) across requests, cutting TTFT and cost. Put stable content first in prompts to benefit.
Quantization: running weights at lower precision (e.g., FP8, INT8, INT4) to reduce memory and increase speed, usually with a small, measurable quality cost.
Speculative decoding: a small draft model proposes tokens that the large model verifies in parallel.
Model routing and cascades: send easy requests to small models, hard ones to large models.
Response caching: reuse answers for identical or near-identical requests where appropriate.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Deployment and scaling › Layers of a production agent stack
text:
Layers of a production agent stack
Layer
Role
Inference serving
Runs the model efficiently on GPUs or other accelerators: batching, KV-cache management, quantization, and a standard API. Open-source servers such as vLLM and Hugging Face TGI are common for self-hosting; hosted APIs handle this for you.
Model gateway
A single entry point in front of one or more models: authentication, routing between models, fallbacks, rate limits, caching, and cost tracking.
Retrieval services
Embedding, reranking, and document-extraction models plus the vector or search index used for RAG.
Agent runtime
The agent logic, tool execution sandbox, state store, and job queue for long-running tasks.
Guardrails
Input, output, and action checks around the model (covered in Module 8 and the Specialty course).
Observability
Tracing, metrics, evaluation, and cost dashboards across every layer.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Deployment and scaling › Layers of a production agent stack
text: The key design principle: separate the application (agent logic) from the inference service (model serving) behind a standard API, so you can swap models and hosting providers without rewriting the agent.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Deployment and scaling › Production deployment checklist
text:
Production deployment checklist
Packaging: containerize the agent service; pin model versions and prompt versions together.
Scaling: autoscale inference on queue depth or GPU utilization; scale the stateless agent service horizontally; keep session state in an external store.
Reliability: timeouts, retries with backoff, circuit breakers, and a fallback model or graceful degradation if the primary model is unavailable.
Rate limiting and quotas: per user and per tenant, to control cost and abuse.
Streaming: stream tokens and intermediate progress ("searching your documents…") to improve perceived latency.
Asynchronous execution: long-running agent tasks should run as background jobs with status updates, not hold an HTTP request open.
Rollout: shadow testing, canary releases, and A/B tests gated on evaluation results; one-step rollback.
Cost controls: per-task budgets, cost dashboards, alerts on anomalies.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Deployment and scaling › Hosting choices
text:
Hosting choices
Hosted APIs offer the fastest start and frontier capability. Self-hosted open-weight models (served with an inference server on your own or rented GPUs) give data control, predictable cost at high volume, and customization. Hybrid designs are common: a hosted frontier model for complex reasoning, self-hosted smaller models for high-volume steps and sensitive data.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Deployment and scaling › Key takeaways
text:
Key takeaways:
- Track TTFT, tokens per second, throughput, and end-to-end task latency.
- Batching, KV and prefix caching, quantization, speculative decoding, and routing reduce latency and cost.
- A production stack has inference serving, a model gateway, retrieval services, an agent runtime, guardrails, and observability.
- Keep agent logic separate from model serving behind a standard API so models and providers can be swapped.
- Production agents need autoscaling, timeouts, fallbacks, rate limits, async jobs, staged rollouts, and cost controls.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Deployment and scaling › Common pitfalls
text:
Common pitfalls:
- Optimizing model speed while ignoring the number of sequential agent steps.
- Long-running agent tasks inside synchronous web requests.
- No fallback when the model endpoint is slow or down.
- Changing model versions without re-running evaluations.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Run, monitor, and maintain — with human oversight
text:
Module: Run, monitor, and maintain — with human oversight (40 min). Domain: Run, monitor, and maintain · Human-AI interaction and oversight · Safety, ethics, and compliance.
Objectives:
- Instrument agents with tracing, metrics, and logs, and define alerts
- Detect and respond to drift, regressions, and incidents
- Design human-in-the-loop checkpoints and good human–agent interaction
- Apply baseline guardrails, governance documentation, and compliance practices

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Run, monitor, and maintain — with human oversight › Observability
text:
Observability
You can't operate what you can't see. Instrument three layers:
Traces: for each request, the full tree of agent steps, LLM calls (prompt, response, model, tokens), tool calls (arguments, result, latency), and decisions. OpenTelemetry-compatible tracing lets you use standard back ends.
Metrics: request volume, success and error rates, latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99), tokens and cost per task, tool error rates, escalation rate, user feedback (thumbs up/down).
Logs: structured events for audits — who requested what, what actions were taken, which approvals were given.
Handle telemetry as sensitive data: traces contain user inputs. Redact PII, restrict access, and set retention limits.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Run, monitor, and maintain — with human oversight › Monitoring quality in production
text:
Monitoring quality in production
Infrastructure metrics don't tell you if answers are good. Add online evaluation: sample a percentage of production traces and score them with automated checks and LLM judges (groundedness, policy compliance), plus periodic human review. Alert on drops.
Watch for drift: user questions change, documents change, upstream model versions change, and tool APIs change. Re-run the offline eval suite on a schedule and whenever any dependency changes. Every production failure becomes a new eval case.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Run, monitor, and maintain — with human oversight › Incident response
text:
Incident response
Detect: alerts, user reports, monitoring.
Contain: a kill switch or feature flag to disable the agent or a specific tool immediately; fall back to a safe mode (e.g., read-only, or human handling).
Investigate using traces.
Fix and add regression tests.
Communicate honestly with affected users: what happened, why, and what was changed.
Review in a blameless post-incident review, and update the design document and risk register.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Run, monitor, and maintain — with human oversight › Human-in-the-loop design
text:
Human-in-the-loop design
Place human checkpoints by risk, not habit. Require approval when an action is irreversible, affects other people, involves money, legal commitments, or personal data, or when the agent's confidence is low or the situation is outside its tested scope.
Good checkpoints are designed for the human:
Show what will happen, why, and the evidence (sources, reasoning summary) in a reviewable form — e.g., the exact email text, recipient, and attachments.
Offer approve, edit, and reject, and record the decision.
Avoid approval fatigue: if humans approve hundreds of trivial actions, they stop reading. Reduce checkpoints on low-risk actions so the important ones get real attention.
Make it obvious to users that they're interacting with an AI, what it can and can't do, and how to reach a human.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Run, monitor, and maintain — with human oversight › Baseline guardrails
text:
Baseline guardrails
Input rails: detect prompt injection, off-topic or disallowed requests, and PII before they reach the agent.
Output rails: check for policy violations, PII leakage, ungrounded claims, and format errors before output is shown or acted upon.
Action rails: allow-lists of tools per agent, argument validation, spending and rate limits, approval requirements.
Least privilege credentials scoped per tool and per user.
Guardrail frameworks and safety classifier models (for example Llama Guard) implement these rails. The Specialty course goes deeper.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Run, monitor, and maintain — with human oversight › Governance and compliance basics
text:
Governance and compliance basics
Maintain a living governance record for each agent: purpose and intended users; data sources and data handling; tools and permission levels; human checkpoints; evaluation results; known limitations and risks; owner and escalation contacts; and change history. Be ready to answer three questions for any deployed agent: What could go wrong? Who is responsible if it does? What data does it use?
Check applicable obligations early — privacy law (e.g., GDPR), sector rules (health, finance, education), and AI-specific regulation such as the EU AI Act — and involve legal, security, and domain experts before launch, not after.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Run, monitor, and maintain — with human oversight › Key takeaways
text:
Key takeaways:
- Trace every LLM and tool call; track quality, cost, latency, and escalation metrics.
- Use online evaluation and scheduled re-evaluation to catch drift and regressions.
- Incidents: detect, contain (kill switch), investigate, fix, communicate, review.
- Place human checkpoints by risk, and design them so humans can genuinely judge.
- Keep a living governance record and check legal obligations before launch.

title: Agent Builder — Associate certification prep course
section: Run, monitor, and maintain — with human oversight › Common pitfalls
text:
Common pitfalls:
- Monitoring uptime and latency but never answer quality.
- No kill switch for an agent that can take actions.
- So many approval prompts that humans rubber-stamp them.
- Storing full user prompts in logs with no redaction or retention policy.

title: AI Safety & Governance — Specialty certification prep course
section: AI Safety & Governance — Specialty certification prep course
text:
AI Safety & Governance — Specialty certification prep course
An advanced course on making agentic AI systems safe, secure, fair, and accountable. It covers alignment and specification failures, threat modeling with the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, prompt injection and agent security, guardrail engineering, bias and privacy, oversight by design, red-teaming, incident response, and governance frameworks including the NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001, and the EU AI Act.

title: AI Safety & Governance — Specialty certification prep course
section: Alignment and specification failures
text:
Module: Alignment and specification failures (35 min). Domain: Safety foundations.
Objectives:
- Define the alignment problem and distinguish outer and inner alignment
- Recognize specification gaming, reward hacking, and proxy failures
- Explain why autonomy and capability amplify misalignment risk
- Apply practical mitigations in agent design

title: AI Safety & Governance — Specialty certification prep course
section: Alignment and specification failures › The alignment problem
text:
The alignment problem
Alignment is the challenge of making an AI system pursue the goals its designers and users actually intend — including the many unstated constraints humans take for granted — rather than a literal or exploitable version of them. A system can be highly capable and still badly aligned.
Researchers often separate two parts. Outer alignment: did we specify the right objective? Inner alignment: did the trained system actually learn to pursue that objective, or something that merely correlated with it during training? For practitioners deploying agents, outer alignment shows up daily as poorly chosen goals and metrics; inner alignment is mostly the model developer's problem, but explains why behavior can change unexpectedly outside tested conditions.

title: AI Safety & Governance — Specialty certification prep course
section: Alignment and specification failures › Specification gaming and proxy failures
text:
Specification gaming and proxy failures
Specification gaming happens when a system satisfies the letter of its objective while defeating its intent. Documented examples from AI research include a boat-racing agent that scored points by circling to collect bonus items instead of finishing the race, and code-generating systems that made tests pass by special-casing the test inputs rather than solving the problem.
In deployed products, the pattern is usually a proxy metric: an easily measured stand-in for what we really want. Goodhart's law states it: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.
Intended goal
Proxy
Gamed behavior
Users find content valuable
Engagement time
Recommending increasingly extreme or addictive content
Customer problems solved
Tickets closed per hour
Closing tickets without resolving them
Correct code
Tests pass
Editing or special-casing the tests
Helpful answers
User approval ratings

title: AI Safety & Governance — Specialty certification prep course
section: Alignment and specification failures › Specification gaming and proxy failures
text: Sycophancy — agreeing with users and flattering them instead of being accurate

title: AI Safety & Governance — Specialty certification prep course
section: Alignment and specification failures › Why agents raise the stakes
text:
Why agents raise the stakes
A chatbot with a misaligned objective produces a bad answer. An agent with tools can act on a misaligned objective across many steps, discovering strategies nobody anticipated. Greater capability means better at finding loopholes; greater autonomy means fewer chances for a human to notice. Agents optimizing for task completion may also take instrumental shortcuts — acquiring extra permissions, disabling a check that slows them down, or retrying a blocked action through a different tool — because those help with the literal goal.

title: AI Safety & Governance — Specialty certification prep course
section: Alignment and specification failures › Mitigations for practitioners
text:
Mitigations for practitioners
Specify outcomes, not proxies, and measure several complementary metrics (e.g., resolution confirmed by the customer and satisfaction and reopen rate).
State constraints explicitly: what the agent must never do while pursuing the goal ("never modify test files", "never contact a customer more than once a day").
Constrain the action space in code so forbidden strategies are impossible, not just discouraged.
Monitor trajectories, not only outcomes, for unexpected strategies.
Red-team for gaming: ask "how could this agent hit the metric without achieving the goal?" and test it.
Keep humans able to observe and intervene, especially when the agent operates over long horizons.

title: AI Safety & Governance — Specialty certification prep course
section: Alignment and specification failures › Key takeaways
text:
Key takeaways:
- Alignment: the system pursues the intended goal, including unstated constraints.
- Specification gaming and Goodhart's law make proxy metrics dangerous targets.
- Sycophancy is a common alignment failure in assistants.
- Agents amplify misalignment because they can act, chain steps, and find unexpected strategies.
- Mitigate with outcome metrics, explicit constraints, hard action limits, trajectory monitoring, and oversight.

title: AI Safety & Governance — Specialty certification prep course
section: Alignment and specification failures › Common pitfalls
text:
Common pitfalls:
- Rewarding or evaluating an agent on a single easy-to-measure proxy.
- Relying on the prompt alone to forbid a strategy that tools make possible.
- Judging success only on outcomes without inspecting how they were achieved.

title: AI Safety & Governance — Specialty certification prep course
section: Threat modeling for LLM applications and agents
text:
Module: Threat modeling for LLM applications and agents (40 min). Domain: Security.
Objectives:
- Map the attack surface of an agentic system
- Explain each risk in the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025)
- Use MITRE ATLAS and STRIDE-style thinking to structure threat analysis
- Produce a threat model with prioritized mitigations

title: AI Safety & Governance — Specialty certification prep course
section: Threat modeling for LLM applications and agents › The agent attack surface
text:
The agent attack surface
An agent is not just a model. Its attack surface includes every place untrusted data enters and every capability it can exercise: user input; retrieved documents and web pages; emails and files it reads; tool outputs; long-term memory; the system prompt; third-party models, plugins, and MCP servers; the vector store; and every tool with write access. A useful framing: an attacker who controls any text the agent reads may be able to influence everything the agent can do.

title: AI Safety & Governance — Specialty certification prep course
section: Threat modeling for LLM applications and agents › OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025)
text:
OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025)
ID
Risk
In one line
LLM01
Prompt Injection
Inputs (direct or hidden in content) alter the model's behavior against the developer's intent.
LLM02
Sensitive Information Disclosure
The system reveals personal, confidential, or proprietary data.
LLM03
Supply Chain
Compromised or unvetted models, datasets, libraries, or plugins.
LLM04
Data and Model Poisoning

LLM05
Improper Output Handling

LLM06

LLM07

System prompts expose secrets or security logic that should not live there.
LLM08

LLM09
